title: Developing a Departmental Approach to Reviewing Answers
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the third post of his departmental-support series, Craig Barton challenges the usual way of going through answers, where students tick, then correct in green pen, then are asked whether anyone has questions. He argues this tells the teacher little about who can do what, because students can hide errors and silence is easy. The replacement, planned with a Head of Department, keeps independent practice but has the teacher pick one to three critical questions and use mini-whiteboards to see every student's final answer. The teacher then responds depending on what the boards show, confirming and moving on, or modelling and rechecking with a follow-up question. A Year 10 example shows pairs being asked to adjudicate competing answers. The strength of the piece is its compromise: not every question is checked, but the key ones are, within realistic lesson time.
points: Standard answer review with ticking and green-pen correction gives the teacher no accurate picture of who understands, since students can easily hide errors.
The fix is to choose one to three critical questions in advance, or from circulating, and have all students show their final answer on mini-whiteboards at the same moment.
The response depends on the boards: confirm and move on if secure, otherwise model and set a follow-up question to recheck.
A pair-discussion prompt asking which answer is correct and where the others come from turns wrong answers into thinking.
Barton accepts that checking every question is unrealistic and settles for valuable data on all students for the questions that matter most.
quotes: Most maths lessons involve a period of independent practice, and most of the time that independent practice culminates with the teacher going through the answers. The most common way this plays out is the teacher projects the answers up onto the board, and students are instructed to tick the ones they got right, and then correct the ones they got wrong, usually in green or purple pen.

Students may mark their work incorrectly, copying things down is not the same as learning, and most importantly of all the teacher does not get an accurate sense of who can do what. Even if at the end of the process the teacher asks: Does anybody have any questions?, or Who only made one or two mistakes?, it is all too easy for students to stay quiet, and these misunderstandings and misconceptions remain buried within their books.

When it is time to go through the answers, the teacher would pick out a critical question. This could be a question they identified beforehand that students might struggle with, or contains a twist, or introduces a new idea.

The teacher now has an accurate picture of every student’s effort and understanding for that question. They can then respond accordingly using the approach shared towards the end of the post on the Do Now - in essence, confirm and move on if understanding is secure, model and recheck for understanding with a follow-up question if the boards suggest understanding is not where it needs to be.

If we had unlimited lesson time, we would of course want to see the responses of all students for every question. But I feel this approach at least gives us some valuable data about all students’ understanding without taking over the entire lesson.
Listen to their answer and explanation. If your answers are different, who is correct? If your answers are the same, where do the other answers come from?
